verify_deep.source: crash-consistency court (SIGKILL mid-append) + mounted immutability proof

checks.name: framing
checks.detail: every committed record framed and checksummed

fsync_tax_vs_fuse_tax.note: The end-to-end append (client write + fsync) is the FUSE tax: the FUSE round trip, transaction framing, watermark write, and index replay. The durability barrier itself (orfs_fsync_latency_seconds) is sub-microsecond here. Do not read the barrier as the append cost.

crash_court.method: SIGKILL the cmd/orfscrashtest writer mid-append, then reopen read-write (quarantining the abandoned tail) and verify the committed prefix is unchanged
crash_court.note: real SIGKILL of the cmd/orfscrashtest writer at a random point mid-append, 120 iterations. The court waits for the writer's first committed transaction (a READY line) and then sleeps a random interval before SIGKILLing, so the crash lands inside an in-progress append. The volume is created with a segment size (genesis frame + one 256-record transaction = 42338 bytes) chosen so every committed transaction ends exactly at a segment boundary, so each append begins in a fresh trailing segment whose id is the recovered committed root; a kill mid-append therefore leaves the abandoned tail in a movable (quarantinable) segment. 38 kills left a tail (0 torn, 38 uncommitted), 38 were quarantined (MOVED, never truncated), and 82 recovered with no tail (the kill landed after a transaction's bytes were complete, e.g. during its fsync barrier). This models a process kill, not power loss: bytes in the page cache survive. Truncations, prefix mismatches and recovery failures are all zero; every recovered volume passed verify --deep and accepted one further committed transaction at the recovered root.

mounted_immutability.note: SIGKILL of the FUSE-client audit writer mid-append, repeated 8 times. Each client append is one acknowledged authoritative transaction: the committed prefix stayed byte-identical and the file only grew, so no committed byte was lost or rewritten. verify --deep on the backing passes after the storm.

notes: This is an append-only WORM audit-log sink, not a general-purpose filesystem: JSON events are appended and fsynced, never rewritten, and readers tail the growing file.
The event corpus is a seeded 80/20 hot/cold skew (a handful of users/actions/resources dominate), not a uniform draw, so the tail and index behave like realistic audit traffic.
Records are fixed-length JSONL lines padded to the record size, so one client write is one FUSE write and one authoritative transaction (the mounted size equals the appended bytes).

The durability barrier itself (orfs_fsync_latency_seconds) is sub-microsecond; the ~4 ms end-to-end append is the FUSE tax — the round trip, framing, watermark, and index replay. Both are published; neither is presented as the other.

quarantine_total and breach_total are the audit sink volume's own counters and must be 0: a clean sink run abandons no tail and is never refused growth. The crash-consistency court separately MOVES uncommitted abandoned tails into quarantine (never truncates) — that is not data loss and is not the sink volume's counter.
The tail reader reports whether it actually observed inotify events (method=inotify) or fell back to polling (method=poll); the receipt never claims inotify when it was not used.

The append-to-observation tail lag is dominated by the same FUSE publish round trip the append pays: a reader observes a record only after the writer's transaction is durable, and the FUSE read round trip adds to it. It sits far above the sub-microsecond barrier, which is why the barrier is never presented as the observed latency.
manifested_bytes is the derived .or_bloom/ plane, produced by an explicit `orfs manifest` pass; it is reported separately and is not part of the authoritative log.
